beats.lead: Your body is glowing right now, and you cannot see it.
beats.text: Every human body gives off a faint visible light, produced by ordinary cell activity rather than the bioluminescence seen in jellyfish or fireflies.
beats.note: In 2009, Japanese researchers proved it by sealing volunteers in a completely dark room and photographing them with a camera sensitive enough to detect single photons.

beats.context: roughly how many times too faint for the naked eye this light is. It is real, measurable light, just far below what human vision can register.

beats.text: The glow is not constant. It follows a daily rhythm, dimmest in the morning and brightest in the late afternoon, and the face gives off more of it than other areas measured.
beats.note: Nobody feels any of this happening. It only shows up on camera.

beats.name: Masaki Kobayashi
beats.role: led the Tohoku Institute of Technology team that produced the first clear images of this light, published in the journal PLOS ONE.

beats.text: The likely source is free radicals, reactive by-products of normal metabolism, colliding with fats and proteins in skin cells and releasing a tiny burst of light energy each time.

beats.line: You have been glowing your entire life. Nobody could prove it until 2009.
